Siedlce New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Siedlce, Poland

NOTE: the source page's site-condition field for this record was found to duplicate the unrelated Siedlce Oldest Jewish Cemetery's condition text ('overbuilt with residential and commercial buildings... no traces... no tombstones'), which directly contradicts this record's own narrative describing about 1,000 surviving tombstones and active 1987-89 restoration work. The narrative below reflects what this record's own description actually states, which appears far more reliable. Siedlce, first recorded in 1448 and granted town rights in 1547 (when Jews first settled), developed economically under the Czartoryski and Ogiński families in the 17th-18th centuries; an independent Jewish community existed by the 17th century, reaching 3,072 (70%) by 1820, and Siedlce became an important center of Podlasie Jewish life. WWI-era attacks killed several dozen Jews; population reached 54.7% (16,820) by 1918, settling at 36.1% (14,793) by 1931. Germans burned the synagogue during WWII, establishing an open ghetto in 1940 and a closed one by August 1941, which also held Jews from Kalisz and a group of Roma. The August 1942 liquidation gathered residents at the old Jewish cemetery, where approximately 2,000 were shot, while over 15,000 were deported to Treblinka II; a residual ghetto and forced-labor camp persisted until November 28, 1942. This newer cemetery, likely established by 1807 (though official land purchase documents date to 1926), was progressively enlarged from 1869-1939, with its oldest confirmed tombstone dated 1855 (pre-war sources reference one from 1827); the last burial occurred in 1988. It holds a mass grave of 1906 pogrom victims, and became a WWII execution site itself, with an estimated 3,000 Jews buried across 18 mass graves (1942-1943), alongside Radom transport-death victims and 39 Red Army POWs killed by Germans. In 1944, occupying forces exhumed and burned these mass graves to conceal evidence. Postwar looting used tombstones for roads and curbs; a 1946 Jewish Committee memorial was later followed by full restoration (1987-1989) rebuilding the brick fence and cleaning the grounds. A 2009 commemorative plaque, funded by the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage and Warsaw's Jewish Community, was placed at the entrance gate.
